title: Mixing regimes of the world's lakes
content:
Abstract

Classifying lakes by mixing regime provides a framework for understanding their ecology, biogeochemistry, and impacts of global change. To assess and scale the climate warming impacts on lakes, it is imperative to know the current global distribution of lake mixing regimes. However, beyond a theorized schematic that was last updated by Lewis Jr. in 1983, we do not know how many lakes of each mixing regime there are in the world, nor how they are spatially distributed. Here, we present LakeMIX, a dataset of mixing regimes for ~ 1.4 million lakes in the world that are ≥ 0.1 km2. With these data, we conduct the first empirical assessment of global distributions and occurrences of lake mixing regimes and we compare our findings to Lewis' theoretical framework. Seven mixing regime types were distinguished with a deterministic, physically based model from satellite-derived and re-analysis data (2013–2021) of lake-specific properties. We found that the world is dominated by small and shallow, cold polymictic lakes (58.9% of lakes), while deep, cold dimictic lakes comprise most (44.5%) of the global lake surface area. In mid- to low-latitude regions, seasonally stratifying lakes are more abundant than shallow polymictic lakes (3.2% and 1.0% of all lakes, respectively). Cold amictic, cold monomictic, and warm dimictic lakes are rare (together, 0.3% of all lakes). LakeMIX fills a crucial spatial data gap in large-scale limnological research, especially for the incorporation of small lakes and understudied geographies of remote regions. The data are openly available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30698423.
